title: The Moral Status of Unrealized Intention
paragraphs: Ethical frameworks emphasizing intention's centrality to moral evaluation confront genuine conceptual difficulty regarding how to appropriately assess unrealized intentions, cases wherein an individual genuinely intends significant wrongdoing or virtue but circumstances entirely beyond their control prevent the intended action's actual execution.

This difficulty proves particularly acute regarding prevented wrongdoing, since frameworks emphasizing intention over consequence seemingly must assign comparable moral culpability to genuinely intended but externally prevented wrongdoing and successfully executed wrongdoing, a conclusion many find intuitively troubling despite its logical consistency with intention-centered frameworks.

Some ethicists argue this apparent difficulty actually reflects appropriate moral reasoning, maintaining that moral luck, whether external circumstances happen to prevent or enable intended actions, should not affect fundamental moral culpability regarding what an agent genuinely willed and attempted.

Critics counter that completely dismissing outcome's moral relevance, even when outcome differences result purely from external circumstance rather than agent choice, conflicts with widespread, considered moral intuitions distinguishing between attempted and completed wrongdoing across virtually every developed legal and ethical tradition.

This persistent tension between intention-centered and outcome-sensitive ethical frameworks likely reflects genuine, unresolved complexity within moral philosophy rather than a problem admitting straightforward theoretical resolution favoring either position decisively.

Practical ethical and legal systems typically navigate this tension through intermediate positions, acknowledging intention's centrality while still assigning some differential moral and legal weight to actual outcomes, a pragmatic compromise reflecting philosophy's genuine inability to definitively resolve this persistent theoretical tension.
